captions.instagram:
How do rivers form?

Nobody digs a river: rain does. Rain on a landscape and watch a river network grow, lift sand and drop mud, walk a waterfall upstream, let meanders cut themselves off into oxbow lakes, build a delta, and follow the Ganga from Gaumukh to the Sundarbans.

→ A river is rain and melt running downhill, from a glacier or spring all the way to the sea.
→ All the land that drains into it is its basin. The high ground around it is the divide.
→ Rain runs down the steepest way. Trickles join, and a river network grows from the coast.
→ Every drop lands in one basin. The high ground between basins is the divide.
→ Slow water lets grains drop. Fast water lifts sand first, then gravel and stones.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/riverclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How do rivers form? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Nobody digs a river: rain does. Rain on a landscape and watch a river network grow, lift sand and drop mud, walk a waterfall upstream, let meanders cut themselves off into oxbow lakes, build a delta, and follow the Ganga from Gaumukh to the Sundarbans.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/riverclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/riverclear

In this video:
• Source to sea. A river is rain and melt running downhill to the sea.
• Water finds a way. Every drop runs down the steepest slope, so trickles join into streams and streams into a river: a network that branches like a tree.
• Lift, carry, drop. Whether a river lifts, carries or drops a grain depends on speed and size.
• Meanders and deltas. On flat land the fastest water swings to the outside of each bend and wears it away, while sand builds a point bar on the inside, so loops grow until they cut themselves off as oxbow lakes.
• Water and mud. Discharge is width × depth × speed, with the speed set by slope, depth and roughness (Manning's equation).
• Rivers and people. Cities from the Indus civilisation onwards grew by rivers, and the Ganga is revered as a goddess.
